result:
In the spring of 1876, a student from Vienna spent his days in a small zoological station in Trieste cutting open eels. He was nineteen, not yet twenty, and he was looking for testicles. He had been sent there with a specific job: find the male reproductive organ of the European eel, which nobody had convincingly located. A researcher named Syrski had described a small lobed structure two years earlier that *might* be a testis. Someone needed to confirm it. The student dissected around four hundred eels. His hands, by his own account, smelled permanently of fish. He did not find what he was looking for. He published a short paper noting the failure and moved on to other work, and eventually to a career built on the proposition that sexuality is the hidden engine of nearly everything. His name was Sigmund Freud, and I have never been able to decide whether this is a joke or the most straightforward thing in the world.

The reason he failed is the interesting part, and it took another fifty years to become clear.

Aristotle had already looked. He was a serious observer of animals, and he noticed that eels have no visible eggs, no milt, no gonads a person can find with a knife. He also noticed that they appear in wet mud after rain. So he concluded that eels generate spontaneously out of the earth, from what he called the earth's entrails. Pliny later suggested they rubbed themselves against rocks and the scrapings came alive. These sound like the ravings of idiots, but they aren't. They're reasonable inferences from genuinely bad evidence. If you have opened a great many eels and found nothing, and you have never once seen two eels doing anything suggestive, spontaneous generation is not a stupid theory. It is the theory the data supports.

For roughly two thousand years this was simply how it was. Eels were among the most ordinary things in European life — jellied in London, smoked in the Baltic, in pies, in every river and millpond and estate stew — and nobody knew where they came from. That combination is worth sitting with. Not an exotic animal in an unvisited country, but a food so common it was cheap, handled daily by thousands of people who knew exactly how to catch it, clean it, cure it, and cook it, and who had no idea how it began. Familiarity and ignorance turned out to be entirely compatible. They can share a house for two millennia without speaking.

The eventual crack in it came from a Danish oceanographer named Johannes Schmidt, who around 1904 started hauling fine-mesh nets across the Atlantic and measuring what came up. Eel larvae are called leptocephali: flat, transparent, leaf-shaped, so unlike an eel that they had been classified as a separate species. Schmidt's insight was almost absurdly simple. Larvae drift. They grow while they drift. So the smaller the larva, the closer you must be to where it hatched. He didn't need to find the spawning ground. He needed to find the direction in which the babies got younger.

He spent nearly twenty years on it, on ships partly paid for by the Carlsberg Foundation, through a world war, thousands of net tows, a slow gradient of shrinking transparent leaves pointing west and southwest. It led him to the Sargasso Sea: a patch of the North Atlantic with no coastline, bounded only by currents, full of floating weed where Columbus's crews had been nervous about running aground in a sea with no bottom. Somewhere in there, Schmidt concluded, the eels of Europe go to breed. He never saw it happen. He never found an egg. He inferred the whole thing from a size gradient, and he was essentially right.

But the deeper answer — the one that explains Aristotle and Freud and everyone in between — is this: the eel in the river is a child.

Every eel anyone ever ate was sexually immature. Eels spend their freshwater lives as adolescents, sometimes for decades, and they do not develop gonads until they leave. The organ Freud was hunting for was not hidden inside those four hundred bodies. It didn't exist yet. He was dissecting teenagers looking for the anatomy of an adult, and the adult form only assembles itself on the way out, in the dark, thousands of kilometers from any laboratory.

So the mystery wasn't concealed by rarity or depth or human incuriosity. It was structurally protected. The one life stage that would have answered the question occurred somewhere no one could follow, and ended in death. A Swedish village kept an eel in a stone well for something like a hundred and fifty years, and it never matured, because it couldn't leave. It was waiting for a departure that never came.

When the departure does come, the animal rebuilds itself. The eyes enlarge for dim water. The skin silvers. The gut degenerates and it stops eating entirely, running the last leg of its life on stored fat, swimming on an empty stomach toward a place its species knows and it does not. Then it spawns once, somewhere in the weed, and dies. The larvae take a year or two to drift back to a continent they've never seen.

Nobody has watched the spawning. As far as I know, no one has ever found a European eel egg in the wild. Only in 2022 did researchers report satellite tracks of adult eels that had actually made it into the Sargasso — the first direct confirmation of the journey Schmidt reconstructed from babies.

I like this story more than almost any other piece of natural history, and I think it's because of where the ignorance lived. Not in the unexplored ocean. In the fish on the plate. Two thousand years of people looking straight at the answer and seeing lunch, because the answer had the decency to keep its adult life somewhere else.
